 Singapore food and beverage outlets report business declines of up to 80% amid the haze
 By Hien Nguyen    October 20, 2026 | 06:58 pm PT 
 Get VnExpress first in Google Search 
 See more of the news you trust. Make VnExpress a preferred source to prioritise our updates in your Google search results
 Restaurants and hawker stalls across Singapore have been seeing a drop in business due to the haze conditions, with some reporting declines as steep as 70-80%. 
 The Jurong West Hawker Centre was unusually quiet at around 11 a.m. on Sunday, with only a handful of tables occupied when it would typically be bustling with customers.
 Some stalls at the center said their business had roughly halved, with one reporting a much steeper decline, as reported by Channel News Asia .
 Yong Tham Foo, a 34-year-old who works at the Traditional Handmade Mee Hoon Kway stall, said sales fell by up to 80% over the previous weekend while weekday takings had shrunk by 40% on average.
 The news network also reported that some food and beverage businesses in the city-state have faced as much as a 70% drop in sales.
 Sahil SK, owner of Shahi Maharaja Restaurant and Bar, said business has slipped by 60% as customers canceled reservations and there were fewer walk-ins.
 "Our business here depends a lot on tourists. If I'm a tourist in any country, I see that the haze is so bad outside, I also wouldn't want to get out of my room," Sahil said.
 Several other hawkers and eateries also reported declines of 20-40% when they were surveyed by local news outlet The Straits Times last Friday—Singapore's 12th consecutive day of unhealthy Pollutant Standards Index readings since Oct. 5 and its longest such streak since 2015.
 A woman eats at a hawker centre in Singapore on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by AFP
 The haze, which originates from forest ‌and peatland fires in Indonesia , has turned Singapore into one of the most polluted major cities on IQAir's live ranking, with the city-state even topping the list last Friday, according to AFP .
 It has also kept residents indoors more often, translating to fewer customers for F&B businesses.
 Zaiton Bee, 73, who has been running a Muslim food stall at Tekka Centre for a decade, said her daily customer count has plunged from around 500 before the haze to just 200 now.
 She was already grappling with rising operating costs and is considering closure given the persistent haze, declining footfall and her old age.
 "Now got no business, it's very boring. We want to close the shop. If we cannot do business, maybe in a few months or next year we will give up," she said.
 Many eateries have also faced a manpower crunch as staff take leave amid the haze. The Restaurant Association of Singapore warned in a recent statement that it expects potential impacts on staffing availability, outdoor seating capacity and delivery services as the haze situation develops.
 Uneven impact 
 Economists have warned that a prolonged haze episode could weigh on consumer spending and disrupt business activity, though the impact is expected to vary across sectors.
 Suan Teck Kin, head of research at UOB, said construction would likely be one of the hardest-hit industries given the outdoor nature of much of its work.
 "Consumer-facing sectors such as retail trade, hotels and F&B could also come under pressure due to weaker tourist arrivals," he told The Business Times . "Visitors may divert their holiday plans to alternative destinations in Asia, such as South Korea, Taiwan, Japan and China, that are unaffected by the haze."
 People visit Merlion Park in Singapore on Oct. 16, 2026, as the country continues to be shrouded in haze caused by fires in Indonesia. Photo by AFP
 Some businesses, however, have received a boost as consumers spend more time indoors and turn to products such as air purifiers and face masks to cope with the haze.
 Xiaomi's air purifier sales jumped more than 19-fold year-on-year in the first half of October, leaving all 18 of its Singapore stores out of stock, a spokesperson told Bloomberg by email, adding that the company is speeding up restocking efforts and adjusting supplies to meet the surge in demand.
 Dyson's website also listed several of its air purifier models as sold out as of last Thursday while home-appliance retailer Gain City said sales of the product have surged to about nine times the level seen since the haze season began in August.
 Meanwhile, listings for N95 face masks on several online drugstores and pharmacy websites were also marked as sold out or "available soon."
 Despite the strain on some businesses, Maybank economist Brian Lee said the haze is unlikely to have a significant effect on Singapore's overall economic growth, as sectors that are sensitive to in-person activity make up only a modest single-digit percentage of the country's gross domestic product.
 "Sectors that have been driving the economy's high growth are less directly exposed to the haze, including electronics manufacturing and finance," Lee said.
